prompt.context: Your client is a London Museum which has an encyclopedic range of attractions. They receive 5 million visitors a year and currently break even with £50M of revenues and costs. The government has told them that they are withdrawing £5M of funding next year and the museum has hired us to look at some of their costs and revenue streams.
prompt.question: How should the museum respond to the loss of £5M in government funding? Specifically, evaluate their touring exhibits revenue stream and assess the returns on their capital investments.

clarifying_info.q: What types of revenue streams does the museum have?
clarifying_info.a: One key stream is touring exhibitions. Each year the museum sends on average 12 exhibitions to other museums. There is also a capital investment budget of £6M per year.

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenues from touring exhibits?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues for touring exhibits over the last seven years were: £80K, £70K, £70K, £60K, £40K, £40K, and £50K.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs for each touring exhibit?
clarifying_info.a: The average cost per exhibition is £60K. Variable costs comprise most of the cost — insurance, traveling curator, and transportation.

clarifying_info.q: What capital investments were made last year?
clarifying_info.a: £1.5M in building maintenance; £3M in fixing the main courtyard (most of it spent on advertising that it was fixed); £1.5M on installing security cameras.

clarifying_info.q: What was the return on the courtyard/advertising investment?
clarifying_info.a: The additional advertising brought in an extra 10% of visitors (500,000 extra visitors). Each visitor brings in £3 in contribution from fees and £3 contribution from gift shop profits (£6 total). Assume visitors will not come again and will not tell any friends.

clarifying_info.q: What is the return on the security cameras?
clarifying_info.a: The security cameras are part of a 5-year project with the same £1.5M invested each year. The museum saves £500K on security guards per year during the first 5 years and £1M per year in perpetuity after year 5. Assume 10% cost of capital.

exhibits.title: Touring Exhibit Revenue History
exhibits.shows: A table or chart of touring exhibit revenues over the last seven years
exhibits.data: Year 1: £80K, Year 2: £70K, Year 3: £70K, Year 4: £60K, Year 5: £40K, Year 6: £40K, Year 7: £50K; Average cost per exhibit: £60K; 12 exhibits per year

framework: Diagnose the £5M funding gap: understand the full P&L (revenues and costs) and identify which levers can close the gap
Evaluate the touring exhibits revenue stream: profitability per exhibit, trend analysis, and options to improve
Assess capital investment returns: calculate NPV/ROI for each of the three categories (maintenance, courtyard advertising, security cameras)
Synthesize findings and recommend priority actions to close the funding gap or improve future capital allocation

questions.prompt: Are the touring exhibits profitable on average? What is the trend, and what options exist to improve profitability?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate average annual revenue vs. average annual cost, identify the declining trend, and generate at least 2-3 options (focus on high-revenue exhibits, send to multiple locations, only tour in good years).

math.setup: Average annual revenue = sum of 7 years / 7. Average annual cost = 12 exhibits × £60K.
steps: Net loss per year ≈ £720K − £410K = −£310K (ignoring discount factor; casebook simplifies as average income £410K vs average cost £420K giving a small loss)
math.answer: On average the museum loses money on touring exhibits (avg revenue ~£59K/year vs avg cost £720K/year across all 12 exhibits, or roughly breakeven/loss at the per-exhibit level of £58.6K revenue vs £60K cost). Trend is declining. The program needs restructuring.

questions.prompt: What are the options if the museum wants to make touring exhibits more profitable by sending each exhibit to more than one location?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize fixed vs. variable cost structure. Fixed costs (getting exhibit ready) are sunk once incurred; marginal costs of additional venues are mainly variable (insurance, transport, traveling curator). An additional venue is profitable if its marginal revenue exceeds its marginal variable cost.

math.setup: Compare marginal revenue per additional venue vs. marginal variable cost (insurance + transportation + curator travel).
steps: Fixed setup costs are incurred once regardless of number of venues
Variable costs per additional leg: transportation, insurance for that leg, curator travel
If marginal revenue per venue > marginal variable cost per venue, adding venues is profitable
math.answer: Sending an exhibit to additional locations is worthwhile only if the incremental revenue exceeds incremental variable costs. The museum should model this per exhibit and prioritize high-revenue exhibits for multi-venue tours.

questions.prompt: What was the return on the £3M courtyard/advertising investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate additional visitors, apply £6 contribution per visitor, compare to £3M spend, and compute NPV. Should note non-financial mission alignment even if NPV is zero or negative.

math.setup: Extra visitors = 10% × 5M. Contribution per visitor = £3 (fees) + £3 (gift shop) = £6. Revenue = extra visitors × £6. NPV = Revenue − Investment.
math.answer: The courtyard/advertising investment is a zero NPV project. However, for a museum whose mission is maximizing visitor access, the non-financial benefit of 500K additional visitors may still justify the spend. The candidate should suggest exploring higher-NPV advertising alternatives.

questions.prompt: What is the NPV of the security camera project?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the PV of net costs during years 1-5 and the PV of perpetual savings starting year 6, then compute NPV. Should acknowledge approximations (perpetuity, 10% discount rate) and qualitative caveats (maintenance, replacement cycle).

math.setup: Annual investment = £1.5M/year for 5 years. Savings in years 1-5 = £500K/year (net annual cost = £1.5M − £500K = £1M). From year 6 onwards: savings = £1M/year in perpetuity (no further investment). Discount rate = 10%.
steps: PV of net costs (years 1-5) ≈ £4M (candidate estimate; annuity at 10% for 5 years: £1M × 3.791 ≈ £3.8M, round to ~£4M)
Perpetuity value of £1M/year at 10% = £1M / 0.10 = £10M, calculated at end of year 5
PV of perpetuity at year 0 = £10M / (1.10)^5 ≈ £10M / 1.61 ≈ £6.2M (casebook estimates ~£6M)
NPV = PV of savings − PV of costs ≈ £6M − £4M = +£2M (casebook: actual NPV = +£1.8M)
math.answer: The security camera project has a positive NPV of approximately +£2M (exact: +£1.8M). It is a value-creating investment and should be continued. Caveats: cameras will need maintenance and replacement every 10-20 years, so the perpetuity assumption is an approximation.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the three capital investments analyzed, what other ways might the museum close the £5M funding gap or improve its financial position?

categories.name: Revenue enhancement
ideas: Introduce or raise admission fees for special/touring exhibits
Develop premium membership programs
Expand corporate sponsorships and naming rights
Increase gift shop range and pricing
Add food & beverage concessions or upgrade café
License IP, images, and content digitally
Host private events, corporate dinners, and evening hire

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Review and cut unprofitable touring exhibits
Consolidate security staffing (complement camera project)
Renegotiate supplier and insurance contracts
Share back-office functions with other cultural institutions
Reduce energy costs through efficiency upgrades

categories.name: Capital allocation improvement
ideas: Prioritize positive-NPV projects (like security cameras)
Redirect advertising spend to higher-ROI channels
Evaluate each capital project with explicit ROI threshold
Explore public-private partnerships for large capital works

categories.name: Government and donor relations
ideas: Lobby to reverse or phase the funding cut
Seek EU or lottery heritage grants
Launch a public fundraising campaign
Engage major donors and foundations

recommendation: The museum faces a £5M funding gap that cannot be closed by the touring exhibits program alone — that stream is currently running at a loss and should be restructured to focus on the most profitable exhibits and multi-venue tours.
The security camera project is the strongest capital investment with an estimated +£2M NPV and should be continued as planned.
The courtyard advertising spend was a zero-NPV project; future advertising budgets should be benchmarked against higher-ROI alternatives.

To close the full £5M gap, the museum should pursue a combination of revenue enhancement (admissions, sponsorship, events) and cost reduction, while building a more rigorous capital allocation framework.
risks: Mission drift if commercial activities compromise the museum's public-access mandate
Visitor experience degradation if cost cuts go too deep
Dependency on one-off donors or grants creates future funding volatility
Security camera maintenance and replacement costs may erode long-run savings
next_steps: Conduct exhibit-by-exhibit profitability analysis to identify which of the 12 touring exhibits to keep, grow, or cut
Model the economics of sending high-revenue exhibits to 2+ venues
Benchmark advertising ROI across channels and reallocate the courtyard-style spend
Develop a 3-year financial plan with explicit NPV hurdle rates for capital projects
Engage government and major donors early to explore partial funding restoration or bridge support
